summaryEn: Taiwan's only domestic professional reinsurer — the company insurers themselves buy insurance from. It was state-founded in 1968, privatised in 2002, is now controlled by the Evergreen group, and pays a 6.4% yield on six times earnings after recovering from the pandemic-insurance disaster that wiped out its 2022 dividend.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; reinsurance framing — sole-domestic-reinsurer status, the state founding and 2002 privatisation, Evergreen's controlling 27.32% and the 17.6% ROE credited, but the FY2022 collapse to EPS 0.41 with no dividend paid stated plainly as a solvency-class event, and monthly revenue explicitly disclaimed as meaningless for a reinsurer; FinMind supplies no gross margin for this company and none was fabricated; sector Financials → Reinsurance)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Central Reinsurance (中央再保險, TWSE: 2851) sells insurance to insurance companies. When a Taiwanese insurer writes a policy it cannot afford to pay out on alone — a factory fire, an earthquake, a fleet of ships — it **cedes part of that risk to a reinsurer**, and Central Re is the **only domestic professional reinsurance company in Taiwan**. Founded in **1968 by the Ministry of Finance with NT$15m of capital**, built on the reinsurance department of the Central Trust of China, it **listed in July 2000** and was **privatised in July 2002**. Today its controlling shareholder is **Evergreen International, which holds 27.32% and is treated as its parent company** — a direct link to Evergreen Marine, also profiled in this collection.

The business is the purest form of risk-taking in finance: Central Re accepts premiums to assume other companies' worst outcomes, and its profit is whatever remains after those outcomes occur. The record shows exactly what that means. **FY2022 EPS collapsed to NT$0.41** — and the company **paid no dividend at all that year**, the only such gap in two decades — because Taiwan's insurers were overwhelmed by **pandemic-insurance (防疫險) claims**, and reinsurers absorbed their share. The recovery since has been strong: annual EPS of **NT$2.61 (FY2023) → 3.14 (FY2024) → NT$3.66 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 net profit of NT$1.84bn** against NT$627m a year earlier, and a **trailing return on equity of 17.6%**.

The valuation reflects both the recovery and the memory of 2022. At **NT$34.40 the shares trade at 6.6× earnings and 1.17× book, yielding 6.40%** — the highest yield in this collection outside the auto-finance and utility names. Dividends have climbed back from nothing in 2022 to **NT$1.4 (FY2023), NT$1.9 (FY2024) and NT$2.2 (FY2025)**. The balance sheet holds **NT$59.2bn of assets against NT$23.5bn of equity** with **NT$16.4bn of cash**.

Two data notes matter. **Monthly revenue figures are meaningless for this company** — reinsurance treaties renew on fixed dates, so March 2026 revenue fell 69% year-on-year while April rose 212% and May 170%, reflecting renewal timing rather than business conditions. And **no gross margin is reported**, because the concept does not apply to a reinsurer. The honest read: **a small, cheap monopoly-by-default earning 17.6% on equity and paying 6.4% — in a business whose entire purpose is to absorb catastrophes, and which last did so severely enough to cancel its dividend.**

Central Re was created in **1968** by Taiwan's **Ministry of Finance**, with **NT$15m of capital**, out of the reinsurance department of the **Central Trust of China**. The reasoning was national rather than commercial. A small economy's insurers write policies whose worst-case losses exceed what any one of them can absorb — a typhoon, an earthquake, an industrial fire — and they must lay that risk off somewhere. If they lay it off entirely to foreign reinsurers, then in a genuine catastrophe the country's insurance system depends on payments arriving from abroad, and premium income flows out permanently. **A domestic reinsurer keeps some of that risk, and the capital backing it, at home.**

For its first decades Central Re occupied a protected position, supported by statutory arrangements that channelled domestic cessions to it. Liberalisation ended that. As Taiwan opened its financial markets, the guaranteed flow disappeared and Central Re had to compete for business against the global reinsurance industry — **Swiss Re, Munich Re, Hannover Re and the Lloyd's market** — companies with vastly larger balance sheets and global diversification. It **listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange on 6 July 2000**, and on **9 July 2002 the Ministry of Finance completed its privatisation**, converting a state instrument into a listed company that had to earn its business.

What it retained is a position no competitor can copy: it is **the only professional reinsurer domiciled in Taiwan**, with the local knowledge, regulatory relationships and currency match that implies. Ownership eventually settled with **Evergreen International, which holds 27.32% and exercises control** — placing Taiwan's sole reinsurer inside the same group as one of the world's largest container shipping lines.

Then came the test. In **2022, Taiwanese insurers sold pandemic-insurance policies whose claims vastly exceeded their pricing assumptions**, producing losses that ranked among the worst in the island's insurance history. Central Re, as the reinsurer behind them, took its share: **FY2022 EPS of NT$0.41 and no dividend at all**. That is what this business is — decades of steady premium income punctuated by the years it exists to absorb.

- **1968 (12 June)** — Founded by the **Ministry of Finance** with **NT$15m** of capital, built on the Central Trust of China's reinsurance department, as Taiwan's domestic reinsurer.
- **1970s–1990s** — Operates as the national reinsurer, supported by statutory domestic cession arrangements.
- **Liberalisation era** — Statutory support is removed as Taiwan opens its financial markets; Central Re must compete with global reinsurers for domestic business.
- **2000 (6 July)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (2851)**.
- **2002 (9 July)** — **Privatisation completed**; the Ministry of Finance divests under the government's privatisation programme.
- **2021** — Dividend of **NT$1.8**, the highest in over a decade at that point.
- **2022** — **Pandemic-insurance catastrophe.** Taiwanese insurers are overwhelmed by 防疫險 claims; Central Re absorbs its share. **EPS falls to NT$0.41** and the company **pays no dividend** — the only such year in the record.
- **2023** — Recovery begins: **EPS NT$2.61**; dividend restored at **NT$1.4**.
- **2024** — **EPS NT$3.14**; dividend **NT$1.9**.
- **2025** — **EPS NT$3.66**; dividend **NT$2.2**; operating margin reaches **21.1%** in Q4.
- **2026Q1** — **Net profit of NT$1.84bn**, versus NT$627m a year earlier; trailing **ROE 17.6%**. **Evergreen International holds 27.32% and is treated as the parent company.**

Central Re's accounts show **a small balance sheet doing a job that occasionally requires a large one**.

- **A recovery that has more than restored the pre-crisis level.** Annual EPS: **NT$0.41 (FY2022) → 2.61 (FY2023) → 3.14 (FY2024) → NT$3.66 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 net profit of NT$1.84bn** against NT$627m in the same quarter of 2025. Trailing **return on equity is 17.6%** — high for a financial company, and a direct reflection of a hard reinsurance market in which pricing improved after the industry's losses.
- **The 2022 event, stated plainly.** FY2022 earnings of **NT$0.41 per share** and **no dividend paid** was not a soft year; it was the company doing what a reinsurer exists to do, at a scale that consumed a year of profit. Taiwan's pandemic-insurance losses were an industry-wide catastrophe, and Central Re sat behind the insurers who wrote the policies.
- **Margins improving with the pricing cycle.** Operating margin ran **4.5% (2024Q3) → 9.0% → 13.3% → 4.3% → 16.0% → 21.1% (2025Q4)**, with net margin at **19.2%**. Reinsurance margins move with the price of risk, and the price of risk rose after 2022.
- **Capital and liquidity.** **NT$59.2bn of assets** against **NT$23.5bn of equity** — a **60.3% debt ratio**, which for an insurer largely represents reserves against future claims rather than borrowings. **NT$16.4bn of cash**, and **operating cash flow of NT$3.89bn in 2026Q1** against NT$1.84bn of net profit.
- **A dividend that tells the story.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$0.9 (2018, 2019) → 1.3 (2020) → NT$1.8 (2021) → nothing for 2022 → 1.4 (2023) → 1.9 (2024) → NT$2.2 (2025)**. The **6.40% yield** at NT$34.40 is the highest among the financial companies in this collection — and the 2022 gap explains why it is priced that way.
- **A data caveat.** **Monthly revenue is not informative here.** Reinsurance treaties renew on set dates, so recent months show **−69% (March 2026), +212% (April), +170% (May)** year-on-year. These reflect renewal timing, not demand. **No gross margin is reported** — the metric has no meaning for a reinsurer, and none has been invented for this page.

The financing reality: **a conservatively capitalised specialist earning well in a hard market, priced at 6.6× earnings because the market has not forgotten what a soft one looks like.**

**Stance: Taiwan's only domestic reinsurer, earning 17.6% on equity in a hard pricing market, at 6.6x earnings and a 6.4% yield — in a business that periodically loses a year's profit by design.**

The bull case:

1. **A structural position that cannot be replicated.** Central Re is **the only professional reinsurance company domiciled in Taiwan**. Global reinsurers compete for the same business, but a domestic reinsurer offers local underwriting knowledge, currency match and regulatory proximity — and the policy rationale for its existence has not gone away.
2. **The pricing cycle is working in its favour.** Operating margin rose from **4.5% to 21.1%** over six quarters and EPS from **NT$0.41 to NT$3.66** in three years. Reinsurance pricing hardens after industry losses, and 2022 produced exactly that.
3. **Cheap, with a well-covered high yield.** **6.6× earnings, 1.17× book, 6.40% yield**, with the dividend rebuilt from zero to **NT$2.2** and **17.6% ROE**. Backed by a controlling shareholder, **Evergreen International (27.32%)**.

The counter-arguments:

- **The business model guarantees bad years.** **FY2022 EPS of NT$0.41 and no dividend** is not an aberration to be discounted — it is the product doing what it was sold to do. Another correlated catastrophe would do the same.
- **Small balance sheet, concentrated market.** **NT$23.5bn of equity** against global reinsurers with hundreds of times that, and a risk pool concentrated in a single earthquake- and typhoon-exposed island. Diversification is the reinsurance industry's core defence, and Central Re has less of it than anyone it competes with.
- **The cycle cuts both ways.** Today's 17.6% ROE reflects hard-market pricing. Softening rates would compress it just as mechanically.
- **Reported figures are noisy.** Monthly revenue swings from **−69% to +212%** on renewal timing, and quarterly results move with claims experience rather than activity.

A **hard-market, high-yield** thesis: own a structurally protected specialist while pricing is good, sized for the year it exists to absorb.

Central Re makes money by **accepting risk that other insurance companies do not want to keep**:

- **How reinsurance works.** An insurer writes policies and collects premiums. For risks too large or too correlated to retain — a chemical plant, an earthquake zone, a whole book of motor policies — it **cedes a portion to a reinsurer**, passing along part of the premium and part of the liability. Central Re both **assumes** such risk and **retrocedes** portions of it onward, in property and life lines.
- **Where the profit comes from.** Two sources. The **underwriting result** — premiums received minus claims paid and expenses — and the **investment return** on the reserves held between collecting a premium and paying a claim. A well-run reinsurer aims to make money on both, but underwriting is the discipline that determines survival.
- **Why pricing is cyclical.** After a period of few catastrophes, capital floods in and rates soften. After a large loss event, capital retreats and **rates harden**. Central Re's operating margin rising from **4.5% to 21.1%** over six quarters is that cycle in action — post-2022 repricing, not a change in the business.
- **Why the domestic position matters.** Taiwanese insurers can reinsure with anyone. What Central Re offers is **local underwriting knowledge, New Taiwan dollar denomination, regulatory familiarity and the fact that its capital stays in Taiwan** — the reason a country maintains a domestic reinsurer at all.
- **The reporting quirk.** **Monthly revenue is not a business indicator.** Treaties renew on fixed dates, so recent months swing from **−69% to +212%** year-on-year purely on timing. Only annual figures are meaningful.

The levers are **underwriting discipline, retrocession strategy, the pricing cycle and investment returns**. The strength is a protected niche in a market where a domestic reinsurer serves a policy purpose. The vulnerability is arithmetic: **a reinsurer's earnings are the residual after catastrophes, and its risk pool is a single island exposed to earthquakes and typhoons** — with far less geographic diversification than the global firms it competes against. FY2022 showed exactly how that residual can vanish.

Reinsurance is a global industry in which Central Re occupies a deliberately local position.

- **The competitive set is enormous.** **Swiss Re, Munich Re, Hannover Re, SCOR** and the Lloyd's market write risk worldwide, spreading exposure across continents and perils so that a Japanese earthquake and a Florida hurricane are unlikely to strike the same year. **That geographic diversification is the industry's fundamental economic advantage**, and it is precisely what a single-market reinsurer lacks.
- **What Central Re has instead.** It is **the only professional reinsurer domiciled in Taiwan** — a position created by policy and preserved by the same logic: a country that reinsures entirely offshore exports both its premium income and, in a catastrophe, its dependence. Local underwriting knowledge, NT dollar denomination and regulatory proximity are genuine advantages in domestic business.
- **The cycle governs everything.** Reinsurance pricing hardens after large losses and softens when capital returns. Taiwan's **2022 pandemic-insurance catastrophe** was a market-wide loss event, and the subsequent repricing is visible directly in Central Re's operating margin rising from **4.5% to 21.1%**. The same mechanism will compress margins when capital returns to the market.
- **The perils that matter.** Taiwan sits on an active seismic boundary and in a typhoon corridor. A domestic reinsurer's book is inherently correlated with those two exposures — the opposite of the diversification a global reinsurer builds deliberately.
- **An ownership note.** **Evergreen International holds 27.32% with control.** Placing Taiwan's sole reinsurer within a shipping group is unusual, and worth understanding when assessing governance and capital policy — the same group controls Evergreen Marine, elsewhere in this collection.

Central Re's position is **protected but small**. The industry truth is that **reinsurance rewards diversification above all else**, and a single-market reinsurer earns its returns by accepting exactly the concentration the global players avoid — which is why it can earn 17.6% on equity in a good cycle and lose a year's profit in a bad one.

**Strengths**
- **The only domestic professional reinsurer in Taiwan** — a position created by policy and not replicable.
- **17.6% trailing ROE** with operating margin up from **4.5% to 21.1%** as post-2022 pricing hardened; EPS **NT$0.41 → 3.66** in three years.
- **6.40% dividend yield at 6.6× earnings and 1.17× book**; dividend rebuilt to **NT$2.2**.
- Controlling shareholder **Evergreen International (27.32%)**; **NT$16.4bn of cash** and operating cash flow above net income.

**Weaknesses**
- **Minimal geographic diversification** — a single island exposed to earthquakes and typhoons, against global reinsurers spanning continents.
- **NT$23.5bn of equity** is very small by industry standards.
- **FY2022: EPS NT$0.41 and no dividend** — evidence that a single event can consume a year.
- Reported monthly revenue is uninformative (−69% to +212% swings on renewal timing).

**Opportunities**
- Continued hard-market pricing sustaining underwriting margins.
- Growth in Taiwanese commercial and catastrophe cover as asset values rise.
- Investment income on reserves in a higher-rate environment.

**Threats**
- **A major earthquake or typhoon** striking a concentrated book.
- **Softening reinsurance rates** as capital returns to the market.
- Global reinsurers competing more aggressively for Taiwanese cessions.

- **Catastrophe concentration (the defining risk).** Central Re's book is concentrated in **a single island sitting on an active seismic boundary and in a typhoon corridor**. Global reinsurers manage exactly this risk through geographic diversification; Central Re cannot. A major Taiwanese earthquake would hit its entire portfolio simultaneously.
- **The 2022 precedent is the model, not the exception.** **FY2022 EPS of NT$0.41 with no dividend** happened because Taiwanese insurers mispriced pandemic cover and the reinsurer behind them absorbed the consequence. Any correlated mispricing across the domestic market flows to Central Re the same way — this is what the business is.
- **Pricing-cycle reversal.** Today's **17.6% ROE** and **21.1% operating margin** reflect hard-market rates following 2022's losses. Reinsurance capital is mobile; when it returns, rates soften and margins compress without any change in the company's conduct.
- **Small capital base.** **NT$23.5bn of equity** limits the size of risk that can be retained and the ability to absorb a severe year — the reason retrocession strategy matters as much as underwriting.
- **Reserve adequacy.** An insurer's reported profit depends on estimates of claims not yet paid. Under-reserving flatters current earnings and surfaces later; this is not observable from outside.
- **Reporting opacity for outside analysis.** **Monthly revenue is meaningless** (−69% to +212% swings on treaty renewal timing) and **no gross margin is reported** because the concept does not apply. Assessment must rest on annual underwriting results, ROE and reserve development — not on the monthly and quarterly series that work for manufacturers.

Central Re's outlook is a question about **the reinsurance pricing cycle and the absence of catastrophes** — in that order. The axes to watch:

- **Operating margin as a proxy for pricing.** It rose from **4.5% (2024Q3) to 21.1% (2025Q4)** as post-2022 rates hardened. Sustained margins near that level would confirm the hard market is holding; compression would signal capital returning and rates softening.
- **Annual EPS, never quarterly.** The series **NT$0.41 → 2.61 → 3.14 → NT$3.66** is the real record. **2026Q1 net profit of NT$1.84bn versus NT$627m** is an encouraging start, but a single quarter of a reinsurer's results reflects claims timing as much as performance.
- **The dividend.** Rebuilt from **nothing in 2022 to NT$2.2 for FY2025**, giving a **6.40% yield**. Continued increases would signal management's confidence in reserve adequacy; the 2022 gap is a reminder that this dividend is contingent on catastrophes not occurring.
- **Catastrophe experience.** The unforecastable variable that dominates everything else. Any major Taiwanese seismic or typhoon event would hit a concentrated book at once.

Bottom line: Central Re is **Taiwan's only domestic professional reinsurer**, state-founded in **1968**, privatised in **2002**, now controlled by **Evergreen International (27.32%)** — earning **17.6% on equity** with operating margin up from **4.5% to 21.1%** in a hard pricing market, at **6.6× earnings, 1.17× book and a 6.40% yield**. It is also a company with **NT$23.5bn of equity absorbing the concentrated catastrophe risk of a single island**, which as recently as **FY2022 earned NT$0.41 per share and paid no dividend at all**. Judge it on **underwriting margin through a full cycle** — a cheap, protected specialist whose product is other people's disasters.
